problem.after:
The style pass of a documentation sprint revises each file against the docspec's shape, the worked example, and the writing standard, and nothing tells it to keep what the docspec's Notes orders. It can undo an owner's instruction the writer followed, so the owner gets documentation other than what the owner asked for.

A docspec is the owner's declaration of one kind of documentation the project keeps. Its `## Notes` section holds the owner's standing instructions to the writer, such as a passage to keep verbatim or an outline to follow. In a documentation sprint, a writer reads Notes and follows it. A style agent that did not write the file then reads it once and revises it, so that each section opens with its point, each fact appears once, and the parts follow the shape's order. The style agent reads the whole docspec, but its one limit is to keep every claim's meaning, add no claim, and cut none. Under that limit it may reword a passage Notes says to keep verbatim, or reorder an outline Notes gives into the shape's order. [story:declare-project-documentation](.ok-planner/design/stories/declare-project-documentation.md) promises the owner that whoever writes the documentation writes what the owner asked for.

A drive of that story found this failure during a recent sprint certification, and a merge agent confirmed it.

`/converge` closes a rejected defect issue only when the code no longer shows the defect or the fix lies in a file the run may not edit. An issue rejected as not real, or as a harm the accept list does not count, stays open, so every later run rejects it again and the owner meets the same rejection for veto each time.

A defect issue is an intake entry that the next `/converge` run fixes without asking the owner. A merge agent judges each one as a report. It rejects a report whose code does not do what it says, or whose harm the accept list, the set of harms the project counts as defects, does not cover. The run's calls table shows the owner each rejection for veto. A final step, the owner list, then closes the issues the run resolved.

The owner list closes a rejected issue for only two notes: `gone`, when the code no longer shows the defect, and `left alone`, when the fix lies in a file the run may not edit. Any other rejection gets no close and no new route. The issue keeps its `defect` route, so `/triage-issues` skips it and every later drive, analysis, or defects run takes it up again. The same step already closes an issue as answered when a verifier accepts a fixer's decline as not real. The story [story:find-and-fix-defects](.ok-planner/design/stories/find-and-fix-defects.md) promises the owner meets only the questions that need the owner's judgment.

problem.after:
The file-ownership decision says true-up rewrites no record's body except a live sprint's retired boilerplate, but a later decision also has true-up rewrite documentation sprints and test sprints. The owner picks how the file-ownership decision words its exceptions.

True-up is the suite's administration pass: it rewrites the files the suite owns and leaves the project's records as written. A record is a file that states what was true when it was written, such as a sprint or a closed issue. A sprint, a documentation sprint, and a test sprint are three kinds of plan, and [concept:sprint](.ok-planner/design/concepts/sprint.md) says the last two are not sprints in its sense. So "a live sprint" in [decision:whole-file-ownership](.ok-planner/design/decisions/whole-file-ownership.md) covers neither.

A recent sprint amended [decision:live-sprints-brought-current-on-true-up](.ok-planner/design/decisions/live-sprints-brought-current-on-true-up.md): true-up now brings every plan of the three kinds not yet archived up to the structure and boilerplate the current release reads. That sprint left the file-ownership sentence as it stood. A reader of the file-ownership decision alone concludes that true-up never touches a documentation sprint or a test sprint. The design corpus describes the project as it stands, so a corpus sentence that contradicts a later ruling yields to it. Two wordings comply and differ only in form: one names every exception in the file-ownership decision, and one defers wholly to the later decision.

The ruling decides how the file-ownership decision's Records paragraph words true-up's exceptions.

problem.after:
The tests tool refuses a second recorded run of one test sprint at once while the first still runs, and tells the user to wait for the first to end. The owner chooses whether the second run refuses or waits.

A test sprint is the planned run that writes the project's tests and fixes the code until each passes. A recorded run, `tests run --sprint <path>`, appends each round of the suite to the test sprint's results file: a header, one line per test as its result lands, and a closing line. Two recorded runs of one test sprint at once used to mix their lines into a round no single run produced.

A recent fix stopped that. Each recorded run now takes a lock that never waits, [tests:round_lock](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tests#L2040-L2049), and holds it for its whole round, [tests:cmd_run](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tests#L2143-L2148). The refusal names the run under way and its results file. The fixer chose refusal because a run that waits stalls its session through a whole suite run with no word of why. No design decision covers two recorded runs at once. A wait with a notice and a time limit would add a setting, and [decision:settings-have-no-code-defaults](.ok-planner/design/decisions/settings-have-no-code-defaults.md) has every project's configuration carry each setting.

The ruling decides what a user sees when a second recorded run of one test sprint starts while the first runs.

The tests tool refuses a second recorded run of a test sprint at once while the first runs, and tells the user which run is under way and to wait for it to end. The owner chooses whether the second run refuses or waits.

A test sprint is the planned run that writes the project's tests and fixes the code until each passes. A recorded run, `tests run --sprint <path>`, appends each round of the suite to the test sprint's results file: a header, one line per test as its result lands, and a closing line. Two recorded runs of one test sprint at once used to interleave their lines into a round no single run produced.

Sprint certification of the sixth intake drain sprint fixed that. Each recorded run now takes a lock that never waits, [tests:round_lock](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tests#L2039-L2048), and holds it for its whole round, [tests:cmd_run](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tests#L2143-L2148). The fixer chose refusal because a run that waits stalls its session through a whole suite run with no word of why. No design decision covers two recorded runs at once. A wait with a notice and a time limit would add a setting, and [decision:settings-have-no-code-defaults](.ok-planner/design/decisions/settings-have-no-code-defaults.md) has every project's configuration carry each setting.

recommendation.text:
A second recorded run of a test sprint refuses at once while another recorded run of that test sprint is under way. It names the run under way and its results file, and tells the user to wait for that run to end and run again.

Rationale: Refusal tells the user what happened and what to do, where a silent wait (B) stalls a session with no word of why, which the project's accept list counts as a harm. It adds no setting, where C adds one that every project's configuration must carry. No step of a test sprint needs two recorded rounds of one test sprint at once, so refusal costs only a rare manual retry. Flip to C if owners run sessions that queue recorded rounds unattended, where a refusal drops a round nobody is there to start again.

title: Whether a second recorded test run refuses at once or waits

messages.text:
Adopt the staged change, amended three ways. The goal: every test a test sprint writes or modifies is worked until it runs as quickly as it can while it still proves its scenario.

1. Scope. The speed review reads only tests the sprint writes or modifies. Tests the sprint keeps or adopts unchanged are out of scope, and no speed reviewer creates a tests item to send one back.
2. Stop point. The review walks the ranked slowest list of those tests, testing.slowest at a time, and goes on past the top N until a whole batch comes back accepted with no send-back.
3. No send-back cap. A test the speed reviewer sends back is rewritten again each time; drop the forced acceptance after two send-backs and its `slow` call.

No time budget decides a verdict: the ranking picks which tests the reviewer reads, and the reviewer judges the waste. Amend both decisions that still describe the old behavior: tests-spend-time-only-on-their-outcome and test-loop-fixes-code-never-tests (which says the loop ends when a whole-suite round passes and that the slowest list decides nothing).

options.label: A
options.text: Adopt the staged change, and amend decision:tests-spend-time-only-on-their-outcome so the sprint's loop reviews its ranked slowest tests by a speed reviewer before it ends, with no time budget deciding a verdict.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep the slowest list for the next plan alone, revert the staged change, and leave the decision as it stands.

problem:
A test sprint records each test's seconds every round, but no step inside the sprint acts on them. The owner chooses whether the sprint's own loop reviews its slowest tests for the named wastes, or leaves them to the next /plan-tests as today.

At v30.0.0, docs/testing.md names four wastes: a costlier reach than the outcome needs, setup a test repeats, a shared resource declared where isolation is possible, and work the outcome does not need. The planning reviewer reads each planned test for them, and the verifier reads each written test for them. Both read; neither sees a measured time. The slowest list that each round records feeds only the next plan's planners, as decision:tests-spend-time-only-on-their-outcome says. A test the verifier passed stays slow through the whole sprint.

On the linescout project, the first test sprint's last measured round ran 503 tests in 32.6 minutes. 22 of those minutes went to tests that ran alone because they declared shared resources. The owner cancelled that sprint and started a new plan because the suite never ran fast enough to use; speed is the purpose of the retry.

A change built for this sits staged and uncommitted in this repo (2026-11-01), across scripts/tests, skills/plan-tests/core.md, skills/plan-tests/test-sprint-document.md, docs/testing.md, both cheatsheets, the family CLAUDE.md, and admin/retired-test-sprint-boilerplate.json. It ranks the slowest list by each test's cost to wall time (full seconds for a test that holds a resource, seconds over workers for an isolated test), adds `tests tasks --stage speed` with a speed reviewer that sends a slow test back with its waste or accepts it at a digest of its files, lets a rewrite drop a planned resource, ends the loop only when every test on the ranked list is accepted, and makes `tests complete` check that. The decision above still describes the old behavior.

messages.text: A. The scope bounds the sort too: tests groups or tests window lists only the legacy files inside the scope, the skill files sort tasks for those alone, and the plan records the files outside it as kept, untouched, for a later plan whose scope covers them.

options.label: A
options.text: The scope bounds the sort too: `tests groups` or `tests window` lists only the legacy files inside the scope, the skill files sort tasks for those alone, and the plan records the files outside it as kept, untouched, for a later plan whose scope covers them.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep sorting every file, and add a sort `out-of-scope` that a sort agent records for a file outside the scope, which the plan keeps as it stands and the stamp carries to the next plan.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the current behavior: a plan deletes every legacy test outside its scope, and the owner widens the scope to keep one.

problem:
A /plan-tests run sorts every legacy test file the window lists, whatever scope the owner set, and the sort has no answer that leaves a file as it stands. The owner chooses whether the scope bounds the sort too, and how a plan records the files it leaves alone.

At v30.1.0, `tests window` lists every test file no scenario claims, across every folder the project owns, and the skill's step 6.3 files one sort task per ten of them. The [sort prompt](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-tests/core.md#L610) says the scope "bounds the scenarios planners write, not your sort, so sort every file your brief names, whatever the scope." Its sorts are adopt, port, support, and delete (orphan or duplicate). A legacy test outside the scope has no scenario to adopt it, because the scope keeps planners from writing one, so the sort can only delete it as an orphan or port it.

On the linescout project (2026-11-01), the owner set the scope to the platform folder and said the runtime folder would come later. The window listed 23 legacy files under ../runtime. The three sort agents recorded 93 entries: 77 deletes as orphan and 2 as duplicate, among them processor tests that pass and are the only guard the signal-processing scripts have. The owner chose to keep ../runtime untouched; the session dropped all 93 entries and the sort agents' 10 calls by hand with `tasks item drop`. One sort agent also ran the device tests, which made uv rewrite ../runtime/device/uv.lock, and restored it with git checkout.

ruling.text: A. The scope bounds the sort too: tests groups or tests window lists only the legacy files inside the scope, the skill files sort tasks for those alone, and the plan records the files outside it as kept, untouched, for a later plan whose scope covers them.

title: Whether a test plan's sort leaves legacy test files outside the owner's scope as they stand

messages.text: A, amended. Add testing.setup with its own clock, testing.setup_silence; the test silence clock starts only after setup exits 0; a failed setup fails every test in the round with the note "setup failed"; any output from the suite command resets the test silence clock. Keep testing.silence as small as possible. Encourage every tool under the project's control to log its progress and activity as it works, so long silences are rare. Give a test that has no choice but to endure a long stretch of silence a carve-out: a per-test exception to testing.silence, kept rare, so the project never raises the cap for every test to fit its slowest or longest-waiting test.

options.label: A
options.text: Add `testing.setup`, a command `tests run` runs before each run of the suite command. It must be safe to run again: it gets the environment ready and finishes fast when it is ready already. Its own clock, `testing.setup_silence`, stops it after that many seconds with no output. The test silence clock starts only after setup exits 0. A failed setup fails every test in the round with the note `setup failed` and the setup's output tail. Every chunk of output the suite command prints resets the test silence clock, as a result line does. `/plan-tests` step 2 proposes both keys, and `tests declare` takes `--setup` and `--setup-silence`.

options.label: B
options.text: Keep one clock and start it at launch, and have any output from the suite command reset it, so a suite command that starts its own environment stays alive while that environment prints.

options.label: C
options.text: Keep the current behavior: only a result line resets the clock, and a project that sets up inside its suite command declares a silence long enough to cover setup.

problem:
A test run has no place to get its environment ready, and its silence clock ignores everything the suite command prints. Together these force a long `testing.silence`, which hides a hung test for as long. The owner chooses how a run sets up its environment and what resets the clock.

At v30.1.0, `tests run` launches `testing.run` and starts the silence clock at launch. [read_stream](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tests#L1894) resets the clock only when a result line lands (`last = time.monotonic() if landed else last`, [line 1908](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/tests#L1908)). It reads the command's stdout and stderr too, but keeps that output only for the failure tail. A test sprint's preflight starts the budget's test stack, checks it, and stops it, so nothing starts the stack for a round. A suite command that starts the stack itself must do so inside the silence clock, before its first result line.

On the linescout project (2026-11-01), about 600 planned tests reach a shared test stack whose cold start builds images and starts about 20 services, and about 66 browser tests need Playwright's Chromium installed. With `testing.silence` at 120, a cold start inside the suite command would stop the run. The owner said 120 seconds is already far too long for silence: a test should not run that long, and whatever a test sets working should not be silent while it works. The owner asked for a carve-out for environment setup and provisioning, and approved option A with `testing.silence` 20 and `testing.setup_silence` 300 for this project.

Keep testing.silence as small as possible. Encourage every tool under the project's control to log its progress and activity as it works, so long silences are rare. Give a test that has no choice but to endure a long stretch of silence a carve-out: a per-test exception to testing.silence, kept rare, so the project never raises the cap for every test to fit its slowest or longest-waiting test.
